title: Raga Vadhans
hook: a raga that opens with peacocks in the rain and holds both wedding songs and laments

segments.voice: Yesterday, a hymn in Bihagra, Mardana's salok, and your line was longing at night. When the late reach came, what were you really thirsty for? Day one thousand eighty.

Monsoon rain on a tin roof. Peacocks calling from the fields, that sharp, high cry that carries a long way. That's the first sound Raga Vadhans makes in the Guru Granth Sahib. Its opening hymn, by Guru Nanak, begins with the peacocks singing and a voice telling her sister that the rainy season of Sawan has come. Joy, color, wet earth. And yet, turn further into the same raga and you'll find songs for a wedding and songs for the dead, side by side. Today: Raga Vadhans.
screen: `PEACOCKS IN THE RAIN.` → `SISTER, SAWAN HAS COME.` → `WEDDINGS AND MOURNING.`

segments.voice: Start with the peacocks. In the opening hymn of Vadhans, given here in plain English, the peacocks call sweetly, sister, the rainy season has come. In this hymn the rains are the season of love: the bride hears them and thinks of her Husband Lord. It's yesterday's longing, but the night has given way to rain and color. Now turn the pages. Later in Vadhans, Guru Ram Das wrote ghorian, songs of the wedding horse. In Punjabi custom, ghorian are sung as the groom sets out on his mare, and the Guru's ghorian take that joyful scene and make it about the soul riding toward God. Further on, Guru Nanak wrote alahnian, laments, the songs of mourning sung for the dead. A wedding and a funeral, in one raga. That's not a mistake in the filing. Both are moments when a life goes over a threshold: a bride or groom leaving one home for another, a soul leaving this world. The Gurus set both to the same music. The raga doesn't pick a side between joy and grief; it holds them both. And the Granth treats both the same way, by turning them toward God. The wedding becomes the soul's union with the Lord. The lament sets the loss inside the Creator's order. Tomorrow, a closer look at one of each. Today's line: joy and grief.
screen: `PEACOCKS, SISTER, THE RAINS HAVE COME.` · `GHORIAN: SONGS OF THE WEDDING HORSE.` · `ALAHNIAN: SONGS OF MOURNING.` · `TWO THRESHOLDS, ONE RAGA.` · then, large: `JOY AND GRIEF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold two things at once. Sit, and breathe. Open one hand and bring to mind something glad from this year, a birth, a wedding, a good day. Let it rest in that hand. Open the other hand and bring to mind a loss, large or small. Let it rest there. Don't trade one for the other. Just hold both, and breathe between them. If you pray, you can say Waheguru over both hands. If you don't, simply let your hands stay open. Later, play one Vadhans shabad, and listen for which hand it speaks to. The bell holds the time.
Raga Vadhans. A raga that opens with peacocks in the rain, and holds wedding songs and laments alike. Today's word.
Your line: joy and grief. Today, when someone shares good news or bad, let them have the whole of it before you reply. Day one thousand eighty.

howItsDone: Shabads in Vadhans are sung in that raga in kirtan; Guru Ram Das's ghorian are linked with wedding occasions, and Guru Nanak's alahnian, laments, are linked with mourning.
